title: Skill Gap Analysis
text: A market-wide list of in-demand skills is not informative until it is compared against an existing sample person or persons. This analysis performs that comparison by measuring what employers in NAICS 523 ask for against records of what each member of the project team can actually do, and reports the distance between the two.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text: A market-wide list of in-demand skills is not informative until it is compared against an existing sample person or persons. This analysis performs that comparison by measuring what employers in NAICS 523 ask for against records of what each member of the project team can actually do, and reports the distance between the two.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Method
Demand is identified from 7,074 job postings, all of which list skills. The comparison skills come from an internal self-assessment: each team member rated their own proficiency on nine skill areas, on a five-point scale from beginner to expert. These rankings were then checked against those nine areas from the postings to determine which frequently requested skills fall outside them.
The gap for a given skill is the difference between the level the market requires and the level the individual holds. The required level was identified by how often the skill appears in postings.

section: Market Demand for Each Skill Area
text:
Market Demand for Each Skill Area
The team searched SKILLS_NAME, the full skill list, rather than SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME to allow a more standard comparison as two of the selected areas- Communication and Financial Domain Knowledge- are not software and appear only in the full skills list. The other seven areas are software-related, and the full list is more complete than the software-only list.

PANEL_PATH = Path("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv")
SKILL_FIELD = "SKILLS_NAME"

# Each skill area pattens 

AREA_PATTERNS = {
    "Python":                    r"\bpython\b",
    "SQL":                       r"\bsql\b|mysql|postgresql",
    "Machine Learning":          r"machine learning|deep learning|predictive model|scikit|tensorflow|pytorch",
    "Cloud Computing":           r"cloud|\bazure\b|snowflake|databricks",
    "Communication":             r"communication|presentation|public speaking|storytelling",
    "AWS":                       r"\baws\b|amazon web services|amazon redshift|amazon s3",
    "Dashboard/Reporting":       r"dashboard|\breporting\b|tableau|power bi|looker|qlik|business intelligence|data visuali",
    "Git":                       r"\bgit\b|github|gitlab|version control",
    "Financial Domain Knowledge": r"financ|investment|securities|portfolio|accounting|asset management|risk management|trading|fixed income|derivative|valuation",
}
assert set(AREA_PATTERNS) == set(df_skills.columns), "Area names must match the ratings table"

panel = pd.read_csv(PANEL_PATH, usecols=[SKILL_FIELD], dtype=str)
n_postings = len(panel)

def clean_skill(name):
    return re.sub(r"\s*\([^)]*\)", "", name).strip().casefold()

skills_per_posting = (
    panel[SKILL_FIELD].fillna("").str.split(";")
    .apply(lambda items: {clean_skill(x) for x in items if x.strip()})
)

# Match each distinct skill name once, then map postings to areas
skill_freq = Counter(s for skills in skills_per_posting for s in skills)

    s: {a for a, p in AREA_PATTERNS.items() if re.search(p, s)} for s in skill_freq

    lambda skills: set().union(*(skill_to_areas[s] for s in skills))
)

Analysis
The team has a strong average proficiency in Financial Domain Knowledge and Communication, but there is a gap in SQL and general coding skills that needs to be addressed. The above learning order table provides a clear roadmap for each member to prioritize their skill development based on market demand and their current proficiency levels.


How to Close the Skill Gap
The way the team can close the gaps is a combination of peer learning and external courses. The following are some suggestions to start the improvement process:
External resources can be utilized such as Coursera learning paths, Udemycourses, and other online resources to fill in the gaps. The team can also consider pairing sessions where members with higher proficiency in certain areas can mentor others. For example, Katie can run short pairing sessions for Fuad and Jonathan in Python, SQL, and Machine Learning. Jonathan’s financial domain knowledge can support the others in interpreting finance-specific postings. For areas like Cloud Computing or AWS, the team can pick one shared course and use the course EC2 work as practice.

title: Introduction
text: Students finishing an analytics degree face a market that looks uniform from the outside and is not. Job titles overlap, postings list long and inconsistent skill requirements, and the same title can mean very different work in different industries. A candidate deciding where to apply has no structured way to identify which industry rewards their current profile, which skills would raise their employment chances most, and what compensation and location trade-offs they are actually facing.

title: Introduction
text: Students finishing an analytics degree face a market that looks uniform from the outside and is not. Job titles overlap, postings list long and inconsistent skill requirements, and the same title can mean very different work in different industries. A candidate deciding where to apply has no structured way to identify which industry rewards their current profile, which skills would raise their employment chances most, and what compensation and location trade-offs they are actually facing.

title: Introduction
text:
Rationale
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment of data scientists to grow 35 percent between 2025 and 2035, far above the average for all occupations, with a 2025 median wage of $120,230 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026a)). Aggregate growth of this kind, however, tells an individual job seeker very little: it does not say which industry to target, which skills separate an interview from a rejection, or where an entry-level opening is realistically attainable.
Securities, commodity contracts, and other financial investments (NAICS 523) cover investment banks, brokerages, asset managers, and related financial-investment activities (U.S. Census Bureau (2022)). The subsector employed roughly 1.17 million people in the United States as of August 2026 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026b)). These firms employ analysts continuously for regulatory reporting, risk, performance measurement, and client analytics, which makes the segment large enough to analyse and specific enough to give actionable advice.
Prior research supports scoping the analysis to job postings. Content analyses of analytics job advertisements show that employer requirements cluster into distinct technical, analytical, and business-domain groups. The mix varies systematically by role and context (Verma et al. (2019)). Studies of entry-level analytics hiring similarly find a gap between what programs teach and what employers ask for in postings (Stanton and Stanton (2020)). A product that reads postings directly, rather than relying on generic career advice, will address that gap.

title: Introduction
text:
Scope Revision
The project originally anchored to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. Pulling that slice of postings returned only 59 results, with salary present on only 13, which would not support the compensation and skill-gap analysis planned for Modules 3 and 5. The team measured the adjacent industry codes and re-anchored to NAICS 523. The career pathway, the product question, and the underlying argument are unchanged; only the industry scope moved, and it remains inside Finance and Insurance. The evidence behind the decision is reported on the Data Preparation page.

title: Introduction
text:
Product Framing
The deliverable is a career evaluation product for a job seeker, not a general labor-market report. Every analysis in later modules is included only if it helps a student decide where to apply, what to learn next, and how to position themselves for BI/Data Analyst roles in NAICS 523.

title: Introduction
text:
Expected Findings

Postings will emphasise SQL, Excel, and BI tooling (Power BI, Tableau) more consistently than machine-learning frameworks.
Regulatory and domain vocabulary (risk, compliance, reporting) will appear frequently enough to act as a differentiator for candidates.
Remote openings will be less common than in the software sector, and concentrated in a small number of metropolitan areas.
The gap between market demand and a typical student profile will sit in domain knowledge and data governance rather than in programming.

These are expectations, not conclusions; Module 2 tests them against the MET Employability Career Match data; Module 3 retests them on the WRDS dataset supplied for this module.

This is the current state of the market the product advises on: 7,074 postings for Business Intelligence and Data Analyst roles in NAICS 523, Securities, Commodity Contracts and Other Financial Investments, published on or after 1 September 2025.

title: Market Baseline
section: What The Occupation Codes Do— And Do Not— Tell Us
text:
What The Occupation Codes Do— And Do Not— Tell Us

Read this chart as a finding about the data, not about the market.
An occupational code is present on only 2,357 of 7,074 postings, 33 percent. Within that labeled third, Management Analysts account for 1,991 postings. But the coding itself does not survive inspection. Postings titled “Senior Financial Analyst, AWS GTM Finance” and “Sr Financial Analyst, Inbound Finance Insights” are coded as Models, Demonstrators, and Product Promoters — the third-largest occupation on the chart. On 2,165 postings the provider also overwrote the job title with the occupation name, so the title field on those rows describes a classification rather than a vacancy.
This is reported instead of being deleted because it justifies a design decision that runs through the whole project. The team’s role filter combines occupational codes with title keywords rather than trusting either alone, and this chart is the evidence for why. It is also a caution for anyone building on the same source: a market study that filtered on SOC codes here would silently describe the wrong population.
The practical consequence for a job seeker is narrower but real. Occupational classification in this industry is unreliable enough that filtering job boards by occupation category will both miss relevant roles and surface irrelevant ones.

title: Market Baseline
text:
How Titles Are Written

Rebuilt from the raw posting titles, the panel contains 4,000 distinct titles across 7,074 postings. The most common single title, “senior financial analyst”, appears 122 times — 1.7 percent of the panel.

The three most frequent titles together account for just 261 postings, under 4 percent of the market.
Titles here are effectively unique strings. The practical consequence for a candidate is that title-based job alerts are close to useless in this industry: a saved search for “Data Analyst” will miss over ninety percent of the relevant openings. Searching by skills and by employer returns far more of the real market.

title: Market Baseline
text:
What The Work Pays

Among the 1,741 postings (25 percent) that disclose pay, the median annual midpoint is $112,500, with the middle half falling between $87,500 and $141,500.
Postings that quote pay hourly or monthly are validated on their own scale rather than deleted as implausible, but they are not converted to annual figures, because the conversion requires an assumption about hours worked that the postings do not supply. This chart therefore covers the postings quoting annual pay.
Two cautions belong with the number. First, three postings in four say nothing about pay, and employers who publish ranges are not a random sample — pay-transparency laws apply in some states and not others, so the disclosed group skews toward those jurisdictions and toward larger employers. Second, this is the midpoint of a posted range, not an offer. Read it as an orientation for expectations, not a benchmark to negotiate against.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Where The Jobs Are

A usable state is recorded on 5,135 postings, 73 percent of the panel. New York leads with 726, followed by California (606), Texas (437), Florida (286) and Illinois (260).
That 73 percent is itself the product of cleaning. The raw field mixed full state names with two-letter codes, so New York appeared twice, and it also contained 1,202 postings labelled simply “United States” and 178 labelled “Remote” — a country and a work arrangement, neither of which is a place. Those were removed rather than counted.

At city level New York is the clear center with 783 postings, ahead of Washington (185), Chicago (136), Atlanta (107) and Seattle (106).
Securities and investments remains a concentrated industry geographically. New York alone holds more postings than the next four cities combined, which is a meaningful constraint for a candidate unwilling to relocate — and a meaningful argument for weighting remote-friendly employers.

title: Market Baseline
section: How Much Experience Is Asked For
text:
How Much Experience Is Asked For

A stated experience requirement survives on 1,702 postings, 24 percent of the panel. Among those, the median is three years and the middle half falls between two and five.
The coverage here is low for a reason worth recording. The raw field reported a requirement of zero years on 2,288 postings, but on 2,143 of them the stated maximum was exactly one year — a fixed “0 to 1” band attached to postings titled Senior Financial Analyst, Finance Manager and Accounting Manager. That is a provider default, not a market signal, and leaving it in produced a median of zero years. To prevent this, the placeholder band was removed and instead the smaller, reliable subset was reported.
On that subset, the market reads as mid-career but not closed: only 49 postings ask for less than a year, while 413 ask for five to six and 107 ask for ten or more. A student targeting this industry directly out of a program is competing for a narrow band of openings. The realistic paths are the small entry segment, adjacent industries with more junior demand, or roles where demonstrable skills substitute for years served. The Skill Gap Analysis page tests which skills most effectively close that distance.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Remote, Hybrid Or Onsite

A work arrangement is recorded on 3,126 postings, 44 percent of the panel. Among those, hybrid leads at 48 percent, fully remote at 32 percent and onsite at 20 percent.
This contradicts the expectation was set out in the Project Overview, where it was predicted that remote openings in finance would be rarer than in the software sector. On the labeled subset, four in five analytics postings in this industry offer some flexibility. The contradiction is reported rather than an adjustment to the hypothesis after the fact.
The caveat is the unlabelled majority. “Unknown” is shown as its own bar and never folded into “onsite”, because an unlabelled posting is an absence of information, not evidence of an office requirement.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Who Is Hiring

The employer side is highly fragmented: 2,461 distinct employers across 7,074 postings. The largest single employer, Amazon, accounts for 298 postings — 4.2 percent of the panel — and the top ten employers together account for only 13 percent.
The strategic read is that there is no short list of firms to focus a search on. Breadth matters more than targeting here. Amazon’s position at the top is also a reminder that industry assignment follows the employer record rather than the specific business unit, so some postings sit in NAICS 523 for reasons that are not obvious from the company name.

title: Market Baseline
section: What This Means For The Product
text:
What This Means For The Product
Five things a candidate should take from this baseline:

Search by skills and employers, not by title or occupation. There are 4,000 distinct titles, the most common covers under two percent of the market, and the occupational codes are demonstrably wrong on a large share of postings.
Expect a mid-career market. Where a requirement is stated, the median is three years and fewer than one posting in thirty asks for less than a year.
Flexibility is available. Four in five labeled postings are remote or hybrid, which widens the geographic options considerably.
New York dominates, but not exclusively. It holds more postings than the next four cities combined; remote-friendly employers are the counterweight.
Treat salary figures as orientation. They come from the one posting in four that discloses pay.

The Skill Gap Analysis page turns these observations into a personal assessment: which skills separate the postings a given candidate can win from the ones they cannot, and what to learn first.

Figures and chart design by Katie Bowles. Field normalization and the Module 3 data-quality review by Fuad Babaiev.

title: Career Strategy
text:
What This Page Will Contain
The recommendations are built from findings already on the site rather than from general career advice. The baseline established that job titles here are close to unique — 4,000 distinct titles across 7,074 postings, the most common covering under two percent — and that occupational codes are both too sparse and too often wrong to search by. Where an experience requirement is genuinely stated the median is three years, with fewer than one posting in thirty asking for less than a year. Four in five postings that record a work arrangement offer remote or hybrid work, and the employer side is fragmented enough that the largest single employer holds four percent of the market.
Those facts point to concrete guidance: search by skills and employers rather than by job title or occupation code, treat the industry as a mid-career market and plan an entry route accordingly, use the available flexibility to widen the geographic net beyond New York, and apply broadly rather than targeting a short list of firms. Each recommendation will be stated together with the evidence it rests on and the limits of that evidence.
The skill-gap results will then turn general guidance into a per-person learning order, and the segmentation work on the Predictive Modeling page will identify which parts of the market are reachable now versus after closing specific gaps.

The panel is built from the WRDS jobs_2026 dataset supplied for Module 3: 504,208 postings across 134 columns, distributed as twenty-one Parquet parts with a manifest, per-column coverage report and checksums.

The third and fourth columns differ because several supplied fields encode missing data as a value rather than as a blank. Those cases are set out under Field Normalization below.
The switch is not an improvement on every axis. Occupational coding is substantially sparser and, as found upon inspection, unreliable where it is present. Experience is recorded on fewer postings once placeholder values are removed, though what remains is a number rather than a figure that is extracted with a regular expression. Geography was the single largest limitation of the earlier panel and it improves by a factor of two and a half even after cleaning, the skill fields arrive split into named tools, specialisations, transferable skills and certifications, and education and experience stop being the team’s estimates and become the provider’s.

The date window keeps the analysis current: the source spans postings back to 2014, and hiring requirements from a decade ago describe a market the target user is not applying into. In practice the window costs little — only 192 in-scope postings predate it.

Why this industry, and why a three-digit code
Module 1 anchored the project to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. That code returned 59 postings in total, too few to support compensation or skill-gap analysis, and lead to the analysis being re-anchored to NAICS 523 after measuring the neighbouring codes. NAICS 523 accounts for roughly two-thirds of all analytics postings within Finance and Insurance, so it is where the market actually is.
The assignment asks for four- or six-digit codes where possible. The earlier source carried no four-digit granularity beneath 523; this dataset does expose NAICS4 through NAICS6, and those columns are retained in the panel for finer analysis, but 523 remains the scope boundary so that the project stays comparable across modules.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Role Definition
The assignment allows title keywords, SOC or O*NET mappings, skills logic, or a combination, provided the choice is explained. For this analysis, the team uses a combination, and this dataset makes the case stronger than before: occupation codes are present on only a third of postings, so an occupation-only filter would discard two postings in three unseen.
A posting is kept when either condition holds:

its SOC occupation matches one of: data scientist, database architect, statistician, mathematician, operations research, market research analyst, financial and investment analyst, credit analyst, management analyst
or its title contains one of: analyst, analytics, data, business intelligence, BI, reporting, SQL, data science, machine learning

Information-security roles are then removed. They match the word “analyst” but belong to a different career pathway, and including them would distort the skill profile the product reports.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Cleaning Decisions
Cleaning stays conservative. Where a value is implausible a blank is inserted into that field rather than an assumed a replacement, and where a whole posting is questionable it is recorded as a gap. Deleting rows narrows the sample; blanking one field costs only that field.
The rules below were written for Module 2 by Katie Bowles and carried over unchanged; only the column names differ, and the salary handling is extended because this dataset quotes pay in several periods.
Duplicates. Deduplicated on the posting identifier. None remained.
Rows missing essentials. A posting is dropped if it has no identifier, title, employer or publication date. After the date filter, none failed this test.
Dates. Parsed to a single format. Where an expiry date preceded the publication date the expiry would be blanked, since one of the two must be wrong and it cannot be determined which is incorrect; no postings were affected.
Salary. The provider’s SALARY column turned out to be a free-text summary whose value is an empty placeholder on most rows, so it is kept for reference but never used as a figure. The usable numbers are the structured range, and that range is quoted in different periods — 1,751 annual, 315 hourly, 18 monthly. Each is validated against bounds appropriate to its own period rather than a single annual rule, which had been silently deleting hourly rates as “implausible”. Reversed ranges are swapped, zeros treated as missing, and 20 rows were cleared as out of range across all periods.
Hourly and monthly rates are kept in their own columns and are not converted to annual figures, because the conversion requires an assumption about hours worked that the postings do not supply. ANNUAL_SALARY_MID — the midpoint of the annual range — is the field used for salary analysis, and it is populated on 1,741 postings.
Experience and education. Taken directly from the provider’s coded fields. Unlike the earlier panel these are not team estimates, so no parsing decisions were needed.
Skills. Arrive as arrays and are stored as semicolon-separated strings across four fields: all skills, named software, specialised skills and transferable skills, plus certifications. Names are not yet normalised, so casing and synonyms remain distinct; that normalisation belongs to the skill-gap work, where it has an analytical purpose.
Remote status. Never inferred, and category labels are normalised because the source spells the same category two ways. A posting with no remote label is an absence of information, not evidence of an office requirement.
Location. Text fields trimmed of stray whitespace. This dataset carries no coordinates, so the latitude and longitude check from the earlier pipeline does not apply; geography is carried by state, city and metropolitan area.
Types. Every column is cast explicitly — dates, booleans, numbers and categories — so later analysis cannot silently treat a number as text.

Field Normalization
Integration testing in Module 3 exposed four defects that coverage statistics alone do not reveal. Each repair is written to a separate column, so the provider’s original value stays auditable.
The job title is overwritten on part of the panel. On 2,165 postings — 31 percent — TITLE_NAME holds the occupation name instead of the advertised title, so a vacancy posted as “Sr Financial Analyst, AWS GTM Finance” reads simply as “Management Analysts”. Counting titles from that field produced an apparent leading title of “management analysts” with 1,991 postings, which is an artifact of the coding and not a fact about the market. TITLE_CLEAN is rebuilt from the raw title text instead, raising the number of distinct titles from 2,396 to 4,000.
Occupational coding is wrong on identifiable rows, not merely sparse. Several postings titled Senior Financial Analyst are coded as Models, Demonstrators, and Product Promoters. The field is kept and the defect reported rather than deleted, because it is the direct justification for defining roles by title as well as by code.
The state field is not only a state field. It mixes full names with two-letter codes, so New York appeared twice — as “New York” (514) and as “NY” (212) — and it carries 1,202 postings labelled “United States” and 178 labeled “Remote”, a country and a work arrangement. STATE_CLEAN expands the codes and discards the non-geographic values, which lowers real coverage from an apparent 92 percent to an honest 73 percent.
Two fields encode “missing” as a value. REMOTE_TYPE_NAME carries a literal “Unknown” on 1,442 postings alongside 2,506 true nulls, and spells the office category both “Onsite” and “On-site”; REMOTE_CLEAN merges the spellings and treats “Unknown” as missing, leaving 44 percent labelled. MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE reports zero years on 2,288 postings, but on 2,143 of them the stated maximum is exactly one — a fixed “0 to 1” band attached to postings titled Senior Financial Analyst, Finance Manager and Accounting Manager. That is a provider default, and left in place it produced a median requirement of zero years across the panel. MIN_YEARS_EXP_CLEAN removes the band, leaving 1,702 postings with a stated requirement and a median of three years.
Several headline numbers fall as a result. That is the intended outcome: the higher figures counted placeholders as data.

Four limitations shape how the analysis pages should be read.
Salary is disclosed on one posting in four. Employers who publish pay ranges are not a random sample — pay-transparency law applies in some states and not others — so the disclosed group likely skews toward those jurisdictions and toward larger employers. Every salary figure in this project describes that subset, not the market.
Occupation codes are sparse and partly wrong. Only a third of postings carry a SOC occupation, and within that third the classification misassigns senior finance roles badly enough to be caught by eye. Any breakdown by occupation describes the coded third, and comparisons between occupations are ratios within that subset rather than counts of the whole market.
Titles are dependable, classifications are not. Raw title text is present on every posting and is what is counted. Provider-normalised titles and occupation codes are used only where the analysis is explicitly about data quality.
Experience survives on one posting in four. The provider supplies a value more often than that, but most of the additional rows carry a placeholder band rather than a requirement. It is a reliable number where present, but absence is common and should not be read as “no experience required”.
Against that, geography and skills are close to complete, which means the location analysis and the skill-gap work — the parts the product most depends on — rest on much firmer ground than the compensation analysis does.

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Product Question

Which skills, locations, and role variants give an early-career candidate the strongest entry into Business Intelligence / Data Analyst roles at U.S. securities and investment firms (NAICS 523), and which skills are missing from a current student profile?

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Why This Industry
Securities, commodity contracts, and other financial investment activities (NAICS 523) run continuous reporting, risk, performance-attribution, and client-analytics functions that are staffed by business intelligence and data analyst roles rather than by research scientists. Because investment analytics is shaped by regulatory reporting and legacy data infrastructure, its skill profile differs from the software sector — SQL, data governance, and domain knowledge often matter as much as machine-learning depth. The subsector is also the single largest source of analytics postings within Finance and Insurance in the data source, which makes the scope both coherent and large enough to support a decision-oriented product.

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Scope Revision
Module 1 anchored the project to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. When pulled in Module 2, the data returned 59 postings in total, of which 13 carried salary information — too thin to support the planned skill-gap and compensation analysis later in the project. Because of that the team measured the neighbouring industry codes and moved the anchor to NAICS 523, which keeps the project inside Finance and Insurance while providing 15,176 postings, of which 6,199 matched our career pathway. Module 3 rebuilt the panel from the supplied WRDS dataset on the same scope: 24,914 postings in NAICS 523 and 7,074 after the role filter. The measurement and the filter rule are documented on the Data Preparation page.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
The earlier pages describe what the market looks like. This page asks a narrower question: can the structure of the market be learned from the postings themselves, rather than read off summary tables?
Two directions are planned against the cleaned panel of 7,074 postings.
Segmenting the market. Postings carry skills, experience requirements, salary, remote status and location. Clustering them should reveal whether analytics work in NAICS 523 splits into recognisable groups — for example a reporting-and-BI cluster distinct from a quantitative-research cluster — and whether those groups differ in what they pay and how much experience they demand. If they do, a candidate can aim at a segment rather than at the market as a whole.
Reading the descriptions. Skill tags come from the data provider and cover every posting in the panel, but the free-text descriptions hold requirements the tags miss. Extracting terms directly from the text lets us check the tags rather than trust them.
Both feed the Career Strategy page: a segment a candidate can realistically enter is more useful advice than an average taken across the whole market.
